name: Deal with garden pests without spraying
blurb: Identify first, then act proportionately. Most pest panic leads to spraying something that kills the predators along with the pest and makes next year worse.
gear: Physical barriers: fleece, copper tape, collars
steps: Identify what you actually have before doing anything. Half of suspected pests are harmless or already being eaten.
Learn the main offenders in your area — aphids, slugs, cabbage white caterpillars, vine weevil — and their natural predators.
Use physical barriers first: netting for brassicas, fleece for carrot fly, collars for cabbages.
Encourage predators with flowers, a pond and undisturbed corners. Ladybirds and birds do more than you can.
Deal with aphids with a strong jet of water and patience; they collapse once predators arrive.
Accept some damage. A garden with zero pests has no predators either.
tips: Broad-spectrum sprays kill pollinators and predators, and pests rebound faster than their predators do.
Slug pellets containing metaldehyde are banned in many places and harm wildlife. Use barriers, traps or nematodes.
proof: You get a crop through a season with barriers and predators rather than sprays.
